title: Cumae. Daedalus. Sibylla
titleEn: Cumae, the Doors of Daedalus and the Sibyl's Frenzy — Aeneid VI.1–97
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The fleet runs in to Cumae on the Italian coast. The ships are moored stern to the shore, the young men leap out to find fire and game and water, and Aeneas goes up to the citadel of Apollo and the huge cave of the Sibyl, where the god breathes his mind and spirit into the seer and opens the future. Before the temple he stops to look at the doors, which Daedalus made after his flight from Crete: the death of Androgeos and the Athenian tribute, the Cretan shore with the bull, Pasiphae, the Minotaur and the labyrinth, and the thread by which Daedalus himself unravelled it for the princess's love. Twice he tried to carve the fall of Icarus, and twice his hands failed him. Achates comes back with the priestess, Deiphobe, daughter of Glaucus, who tells Aeneas that this is no time for sights and orders a sacrifice. She leads the Trojans into the cave, with its hundred mouths and hundred voices. At the threshold the god takes hold of her: her face, colour and hair change, her breast heaves, and she cries that the god is here and rebukes Aeneas for hanging back from his prayers. Aeneas prays to Apollo, who guided Paris's arrow into Achilles, recalls the seas and peoples he has crossed, asks that Troy's ill fortune end here, begs a home in Latium for the Trojans and their wandering gods, and promises a marble temple, festivals and a shrine for her oracles; only let her not write them on leaves for the winds to scatter, but speak them herself. The Sibyl rages in the cave, struggling against the god, who bridles her; then the hundred doors open of themselves and she gives her answer. The sea is behind him; heavier trials wait on land. The Trojans will come to the realm of Lavinium, and will wish they had not. She sees wars and the Tiber foaming with blood, a second Achilles, born of a goddess, and Juno never absent; the cause will be a foreign bride again. Aeneas must not yield to misfortune but go against it more boldly, and the first road to safety will open from a Greek city, where he least expects it.
part: Cumae, the Doors of Daedalus and the Sibyl's Frenzy (VI.1–97)

sentences.t:
Sic fatur lacrimans, classique immittit habenas,
et tandem Euboïcis Cumarum adlabitur oris.
sentences.l:
So he speaks, weeping, and lets the reins go slack to the fleet,
and at last glides on to the Euboean shores of Cumae.
sentences.i: So he spoke, in tears, and gave his fleet its head, and at last it glided in to the Euboean shore at Cumae.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the opening of Book VI; 'sic' looks back to the lament that ends Book V, so this is Aeneas, still mourning Palinurus. 'Fatur' is a present of the deponent 'for', 'speaks', which you'll see constantly in a narrative present. 'Classi… immittit habenas' is 'lets the reins go to the fleet': 'classi' is a dative, and the picture is of a rider slackening the reins of a horse. 'Adlabitur' is Greenough's spelling of 'allabitur', 'glides up to', and 'oris' is a dative of the place reached ('to the shores'). Cumae was founded by Greeks from Chalcis in Euboea, hence 'Euboïcis'; Greenough prints a diaeresis on the 'i' to show that the word has four syllables, and the Latin Library drops it (orthography only).

sentences.t: Obvertunt pelago proras;
sentences.l: They turn their prows to the sea;
sentences.i: They swing the prows round to face the sea;
sentences.n: 'Obvertunt' is 'turn toward', and 'pelago' (dative) is what the prows face; the ships are being brought in stern-first. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
tum dente tenaci
ancora fundabat naves, et litora curvae
praetexunt puppes.
sentences.l:
then with its gripping tooth
the anchor was holding the ships, and the curved sterns
fringe the shores.
sentences.i: Then the anchor's gripping fluke held the ships fast, and the curving sterns made a border along the shore.
sentences.n: 'Dente tenaci' is an ablative of means: the anchor's fluke is its 'tooth'. 'Ancora' is a singular noun standing for one anchor to each ship. 'Fundabat' is an imperfect of 'fundo, -are', 'to make fast', not the verb 'fundo, -ere', 'pour' (the two are different verbs). 'Naves' is Greenough's accusative plural in '-es'; the Latin Library prints 'navis', which is the same case. 'Praetexunt' is literally 'weave a border in front of', a picture of the line of hulls fringing the shore like the edge of a cloth; the tense moves from the imperfect to the present, a vivid shift.

sentences.t:
Iuvenum manus emicat ardens
litus in Hesperium;
sentences.l:
The band of young men leaps out, eager,
onto the Hesperian shore;
sentences.i: The band of young men springs out in eager haste upon the Western shore;
sentences.n: 'Iuvenum' is the genitive plural of 'iuvenis' (the ordinary form, with '-um'). 'Manus' is a feminine noun meaning a 'band' of men, and it has a singular verb. 'Emicat' is 'darts out', 'leaps forth'. 'Hesperium' is 'western', that is Italy, the land to the west of Greece; the word was Greek in origin and is used by Virgil as a name for Italy.

sentences.t:
quaerit pars semina flammae
abstrusa in venis silicis, pars densa ferarum
tecta rapit silvas, inventaque flumina monstrat.
sentences.l:
one part seeks the seeds of flame
hidden in the veins of flint, another part the dense
dwellings of wild beasts plunders, the woods, and points out found streams.
sentences.i: Some look for the sparks of fire hidden in the veins of flint; others ransack the woods, the thick lairs of wild beasts, and point out the streams they find.
sentences.n: 'Pars… pars' is 'some… others', each with a singular verb. 'Semina flammae' is 'seeds of flame', sparks (the idiom is Lucretian). 'Abstrusa' is a perfect participle passive of 'abstrudo', 'hidden away', agreeing with 'semina'. 'Densa ferarum tecta' is 'the thick coverts of wild beasts', 'ferarum' the genitive plural of 'fera'; 'silvas' is best taken as standing in apposition to 'tecta', 'the woods'. 'Rapit' is 'seizes', 'plunders', here meaning a hurried search. 'Inventaque flumina' is 'and the streams once found', 'inventa' a perfect participle passive neuter plural.

sentences.t:
At pius Aeneas arces, quibus altus Apollo
praesidet, horrendaeque procul secreta Sibyllae
antrum immane petit, magnum cui mentem animumque
Delius inspirat vates, aperitque futura.
sentences.l:
But pious Aeneas the heights, over which high Apollo
presides, and the secret places of the dread Sibyl far off,
the huge cave seeks, into whom mightily mind and spirit
the Delian seer breathes, and opens the things to come.
sentences.i: But devout Aeneas makes for the heights where Apollo sits enthroned and for the remote recess of the dread Sibyl, her vast cave; the Delian god breathes mind and spirit into her mightily and unfolds the future.
sentences.n: 'Pius' is Aeneas's constant epithet: dutiful to gods, family and country. The object of 'petit' is split in two, 'arces… quibus' with its own relative clause, and 'antrum immane', with 'secreta' ('hidden places', neuter plural noun) and 'horrendae… Sibyllae' ('to be shuddered at') in between. 'Praesidet' takes the dative 'quibus', 'presides over'. 'Cui' is dative, 'into whom', with 'inspirat'; Greenough's 'magnum' can be read as an adverb, 'mightily', while the Latin Library's 'magnam' would agree with 'mentem'. 'Delius vates' is Apollo, 'the Delian seer', born on Delos. 'Futura' is the neuter plural of the future participle, 'things to come', used as a noun.

sentences.t: Iam subeunt Triviae lucos atque aurea tecta.
sentences.l: Now they go up to Trivia's groves and the golden roof.
sentences.i: Now they climb to the groves of Trivia and the golden temple.
sentences.n: 'Trivia' ('of the crossroads') is a title of Diana, here the goddess whom the Sibyl serves along with Apollo (see 35). 'Subeunt' takes the accusative, 'go up to', 'approach'. 'Aurea tecta' is Apollo's golden temple, which the next lines say Daedalus built.

sentences.t:
Daedalus, ut fama est, fugiens Minoïa regna,
praepetibus pennis ausus se credere caelo,
insuetum per iter gelidas enavit ad Arctos,
Chalcidicaque levis tandem super adstitit arce.
sentences.l:
Daedalus, as the tale is, fleeing the Minoan kingdom,
having dared to trust himself to the sky on swift wings,
by a strange path swam out to the cold Bears,
and lightly stood at last above the Chalcidian citadel.
sentences.i: Daedalus, so the story goes, fleeing the realm of Minos, dared to entrust himself to the air on swift wings, flew by an untried road to the cold north, and came lightly to rest at last on the Chalcidian height.
sentences.n: 'Ut fama est' is a parenthesis, 'as the story goes'. 'Minoïa regna' is the realm of Minos, Crete, from which Daedalus escaped; Greenough prints the diaeresis (the Latin Library drops it). 'Ausus' is the perfect participle of the semi-deponent 'audeo', 'having dared', with an infinitive 'se credere'. 'Praepetibus pennis' is an ablative of means, 'on swift wings'. 'Insuetum per iter' is 'per insuetum iter', the preposition set between adjective and noun. 'Enavit' is 'swam out', a verb of swimming used of flight. 'Gelidas… Arctos' is the northern Bears, so the north. 'Levis' is a predicative nominative, 'lightly'. 'Chalcidica arce' is the citadel of Cumae, a colony from Chalcis; 'adstitit' is Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library prints 'astitit').

sentences.t:
Redditus his primum terris, tibi, Phoebe, sacravit
remigium alarum, posuitque immania templa.
sentences.l:
Restored first to these lands, to you, Phoebus, he consecrated
the oar-gear of his wings, and set up huge temples.
sentences.i: Set down on these shores, he first dedicated to you, Phoebus, the oarage of his wings, and put up a mighty temple.
sentences.n: 'Redditus' is a perfect participle passive of 'reddo', 'given back'; 'his… terris' is a poetic dative of the place reached. 'Primum' is 'first'. 'Remigium alarum' is 'the rowing-gear of the wings', a figure of speech that makes the wings oars. 'Phoebe' is a vocative. 'Posuit' is 'set up'; 'immania templa' is a plural for a single temple (poetic plural).

sentences.t: In foribus letum Androgeo:
sentences.l: On the doors, the death of Androgeos:
sentences.i: On the doors is carved the death of Androgeos:
sentences.n: The temple doors are carved in relief, and Virgil describes the scenes in order. There is no verb, only 'letum', 'the death'; 'est' is understood. 'Androgeo' is the Greek genitive in '-o', 'of Androgeos'. He was Minos's son, killed in Athens, and for his death Minos exacted the tribute described next. The colon opens the account.

sentences.i: then the Athenians, ordered to pay the penalty — a pitiable thing — seven bodies of their sons every year;
sentences.n: 'Cecropidae' is 'the sons of Cecrops', the Athenians (Cecrops was an early king of Athens); it is nominative plural, Greek in form. 'Iussi' is a perfect participle passive, 'ordered', taking 'pendere poenas', 'to pay the penalty', the idiom for paying a fine. 'Miserum!' is a neuter exclamation set between dashes, 'a wretched thing'. 'Septena' is a distributive, 'seven at a time', and 'septena corpora natorum' says what the penalty was, 'bodies of sons' ('natorum' genitive plural of 'natus'); 'quotannis' is 'every year'.

sentences.t: stat ductis sortibus urna.
sentences.l: the urn stands, the lots having been drawn.
sentences.i: the urn stands there, the lots drawn.
sentences.n: 'Ductis sortibus' is an ablative absolute, 'the lots having been drawn'; the urn on the door is shown standing with the lots taken. The scene is of how the victims were chosen.

sentences.t: Contra elata mari respondet Gnosia tellus:
sentences.l: Opposite, raised out of the sea, answers the Gnosian land:
sentences.i: Opposite, rising from the sea, the land of Cnossos answers:
sentences.n: 'Contra' is an adverb, 'opposite', the other door. 'Elata' is a perfect participle passive of 'effero', 'lifted up', with 'mari' an ablative of separation, 'out of the sea'. 'Respondet' is 'answers', 'corresponds'. 'Gnosia tellus' is Crete (Cnossos was Minos's city); the Latin Library prints 'Cnosia'. The colon leads to the scenes on this door.

sentences.i: Here are the cruel passion for the bull, Pasiphae slipped beneath it by a ruse, and the hybrid offspring of two natures, the Minotaur, reminders of a lust beyond naming;
sentences.n: 'Hic' is 'here', on this door, and the verb 'inest', 'is in it', stays singular for a string of subjects. 'Amor tauri' is 'love of the bull', Pasiphae's passion for the bull. 'Suppostaque' is the syncopated 'suppositaque', a perfect participle passive of 'suppono', 'put under', with 'furto', 'by a trick', an ablative; Pasiphaë has a diaeresis in Greenough (the Latin Library prints 'Pasiphae'). 'Mixtum genus' and 'proles biformis' ('biformis' is the nominative feminine in '-is') are in apposition to 'Minotaurus'. 'Veneris… nefandae' is 'of unspeakable Venus', Venus meaning lust, and 'monumenta' are 'reminders' (the Latin Library prints 'monimenta').

sentences.t: hic labor ille domus et inextricabilis error;
sentences.l: here that famous toil of the house, and the unthreadable wandering;
sentences.i: Here too is the famed toil of the building, the winding that no one can unravel;
sentences.n: 'Hic' is 'here' again and 'inest' is understood. 'Labor ille domus' is 'that famous toil of the house', the labyrinth; 'ille' is used for something well known. 'Inextricabilis error' is 'a wandering that cannot be untangled', the maze as a state of being lost.

sentences.t:
magnum reginae sed enim miseratus amorem
Daedalus ipse dolos tecti ambagesque resolvit,
caeca regens filo vestigia.
sentences.l:
but indeed, the great love of the queen pitying,
Daedalus himself the tricks of the building and the windings unravelled,
guiding the blind footsteps with a thread.
sentences.i: But Daedalus himself, moved to pity by the princess's great love, undid the tricks and windings of the building, guiding the blind steps by a thread.
sentences.n: 'Sed enim' is 'but in truth', an idiom which introduces a fact that explains or overrides what went before. 'Miseratus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'miseror', 'having pitied', with the accusative 'amorem'. 'Magnum… amorem' frames 'reginae', the 'great love' of the 'queen' ('reginae'), Ariadne, Minos's daughter, who is 'the princess' in i: her love for Theseus. 'Dolos tecti ambagesque' is 'the deceits and windings of the building', 'tecti' genitive singular. 'Caeca… vestigia' are 'blind steps', steps of one who cannot see his way, Theseus's. 'Filo' is an ablative of means, 'by a thread'; 'regens' is a present participle.

sentences.t:
Tu quoque magnam
partem opere in tanto, sineret dolor, Icare, haberes.
sentences.l:
You also a great part
in so great a work, if grief allowed, Icarus, would have had.
sentences.i: You too, Icarus, would have had a large share in so great a work, if grief had let you.
sentences.n: The poet turns to address Icarus ('Icare' is a vocative), Daedalus's son who fell into the sea. 'Sineret dolor' is the condition with 'si' left out, an imperfect subjunctive doing the work of the pluperfect, as poets may use it: 'if grief had allowed it'; 'haberes' is the matching imperfect subjunctive in the main clause, 'you would have had'. 'Magnam partem' is an accusative, 'a great part', and 'opere in tanto' is 'in so great a work'.

sentences.t: Bis conatus erat casus effingere in auro;
sentences.l: Twice he had tried to fashion the fall in gold;
sentences.i: Twice he had tried to shape the fall in gold;
sentences.n: 'Conatus erat' is the pluperfect of the deponent 'conor', 'he had tried', Daedalus being the subject. 'Casus' is accusative plural of the fourth-declension 'casus', 'fall', here Icarus's fall. 'Effingere in auro' is 'to model in gold'.

sentences.t: bis patriae cecidere manus.
sentences.l: twice the father's hands fell.
sentences.i: twice his father's hands dropped.
sentences.n: 'Cecidere' is 'ceciderunt' (you'll see '-ere' for '-erunt' constantly), 'fell', 'dropped', the hands failing him. 'Patriae manus' is 'the father's hands' ('patrius' is 'of a father'). 'Bis… bis' is repetition for pathos.

sentences.t:
Quin protinus omnia
perlegerent oculis, ni iam praemissus Achates
adforet, atque una Phoebi Triviaeque sacerdos,
Deiphobe Glauci, fatur quae talia regi:
sentences.l:
Indeed they would have read through everything with their eyes,
if Achates, sent ahead, were not already there,
and with him the priestess of Phoebus and Trivia,
Deiphobe daughter of Glaucus, who speaks such things to the king:
sentences.i: Nay, they would have gone on and scanned it all with their eyes, had not Achates, sent on ahead, already arrived, with the priestess of Phoebus and Trivia beside him, Glaucus's daughter Deiphobe, who speaks to the king as follows:
sentences.n: 'Quin' here is 'nay more', 'indeed'. 'Perlegerent' and 'adforet' are imperfect subjunctives of a contrary-to-fact condition, 'they would have read through… had Achates not been there' (the imperfect subjunctive doing the work of the pluperfect, as at 31). 'Adforet' is Greenough's spelling of 'afforet', a by-form of 'adesset'. 'Praemissus' is a perfect participle passive, 'sent ahead', agreeing with Achates, Aeneas's faithful companion. 'Una' is an adverb, 'together with him'. 'Deiphobe Glauci' is 'Deiphobe of Glaucus', 'daughter' understood: this is the Sibyl's name. 'Quae' is a relative, nominative feminine, and 'regi' is a dative, 'to the king', Aeneas. The colon leads to her speech.

sentences.t: “Non hoc ista sibi tempus spectacula poscit;
sentences.l: “Not this time those sights for itself demands;
sentences.i: “This moment does not call for those sights;
sentences.n: The opening mark begins the Sibyl's speech, which runs to 39. 'Hoc… tempus' is the nominative subject (the 'time'), 'ista spectacula' is the object ('those sights') and 'sibi' is a dative of interest, 'for itself'. 'Ista' is 'those', with a shade of 'those things you are looking at'.

sentences.t:
nunc grege de intacto septem mactare iuvencos
praestiterit, totidem lectas de more bidentes.”
sentences.l:
now from an untouched herd it will have been better to sacrifice
seven bullocks, and as many chosen sheep, according to custom.”
sentences.i: It would be better now to slay seven bullocks from a herd no yoke has touched, and as many chosen sheep, in the proper way.”
sentences.n: 'Praestiterit' is a form that can be read as a future perfect or a perfect subjunctive; the sense is 'it will be best', with 'mactare' as the infinitive, 'to sacrifice', and the use of the tense as a courteous urgent suggestion. 'Grege de intacto' is 'from an untouched herd' (one never worked), with the preposition set between the adjective and noun. 'Totidem… bidentes' is 'as many sheep'; 'lectas' ('chosen') agrees with 'bidentes', an accusative plural in '-es' (the Latin Library prints 'bidentis', the same case), and 'bidens' is a full-grown sheep fit for sacrifice. 'De more' is 'according to custom'. The Latin Library has 'ex' for Greenough's 'de' (the sense is the same). The closing mark ends the speech.

sentences.t:
Talibus adfata Aenean (nec sacra morantur
iussa viri), Teucros vocat alta in templa sacerdos.
sentences.l:
Having addressed Aeneas with such words (nor do the men delay the sacred
commands), the priestess calls the Teucrians into the high temple.
sentences.i: With such words she addressed Aeneas (and the men do not delay the sacred bidding), and the priestess calls the Trojans into the lofty temple.
sentences.n: 'Adfata' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'adfor', 'having spoken to', with the accusative 'Aenean' (a Greek accusative in '-an'); its subject, 'sacerdos', is held back to the last word. 'Talibus' is an ablative of means, 'with such words'. The parenthesis 'nec sacra morantur iussa viri' is 'nor do the men delay the sacred commands': 'morantur' is the deponent 'moror', 'delay', and 'viri' is nominative plural. 'Alta in templa' has the preposition between adjective and noun. 'Teucros' are the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.

sentences.t:
Excisum Euboicae latus ingens rupis in antrum,
quo lati ducunt aditus centum, ostia centum;
sentences.l:
A huge flank of the Euboean rock is cut into a cave,
to which lead a hundred broad passages, a hundred mouths;
sentences.i: The vast flank of the Euboean cliff has been hollowed into a cavern, which a hundred wide passages lead to, a hundred doorways;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. There is no main verb: 'est' is understood. 'Excisum' is a perfect participle passive, neuter, agreeing with 'latus', 'a flank cut out', with 'Euboicae rupis' ('of the Euboean rock', the cliff of Cumae) and 'in antrum' ('into a cave'). 'Quo' is 'to which', with 'ducunt', 'lead'. 'Ostia centum' is an apposition to 'aditus centum', 'a hundred doors'.

sentences.t: unde ruunt totidem voces, responsa Sibyllae.
sentences.l: from which rush as many voices, the answers of the Sibyl.
sentences.i: and from them rush as many voices, the Sibyl's replies.
sentences.n: 'Unde' is 'from which', 'totidem' is 'as many', i.e. a hundred. 'Responsa Sibyllae' is in apposition to 'voces', 'the Sibyl's answers'. The hundred mouths are also the hundred voices.

sentences.t:
Ventum erat ad limen, cum virgo. “Poscere fata
“tempus ait;
sentences.l:
They had come to the threshold, when the maiden: “To demand the fates
is time,” she says;
sentences.i: They had come to the threshold, when the maiden: “It is time to ask the fates,” she says;
sentences.n: The print has 'virgo. “Poscere fata / “tempus ait; deus, ecce, deus! ”Cui', a misprint for 'virgo, “Poscere fata tempus” ait; “deus, ecce, deus!” Cui': a full stop for a comma after 'virgo', an opening mark for the closing mark after 'tempus', and no opening mark before the second 'deus'. t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i give the reading. 'Ventum erat' is an impersonal pluperfect passive, literally 'it had been come', 'they had come'. 'Cum virgo' is 'when the maiden' (the Sibyl is the 'virgo', the maiden), and its verb 'ait' is held back to 46. 'Poscere fata tempus' is '(it is) time to demand the fates', 'to ask for the oracles', with 'est' left out.

sentences.t: deus, ecce, deus!
sentences.l: “the god, look, the god!”
sentences.i: “The god! Look, the god!”
sentences.n: The print has 'deus! ”Cui', the closing mark of the cry set after a space and joined to the next word, a misprint for 'deus!” Cui'; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source (the mark stands at the head of the next unit); l and i close the cry after 'deus!'. The opening mark before this second 'deus' is missing in the print (see the note on the previous unit). The repetition 'deus… deus', with 'ecce' ('look!') between, is her cry as the god takes hold of her.

sentences.i: As she said this before the doors, her face suddenly stayed no longer the same, nor her colour, nor her carefully dressed hair;
sentences.n: The mark ” before 'Cui' is the misprinted closing mark of her cry (see the note on the previous unit). 'Cui… fanti' is a dative of the present participle of 'for', 'to her as she spoke', a dative of reference with 'mansere' ('mansere' is 'manserunt', 'remained'; you'll see '-ere' for '-erunt' constantly). 'Non voltus, non color unus' is 'not one face, not one colour', 'unus' meaning 'the same' (the face and colour were unchanged); 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus' (the Latin Library prints 'vultus'). 'Comptae… comae' is 'her dressed hair', 'compta' being a perfect participle passive of 'como'. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
sed pectus anhelum,
et rabie fera corda tument;
sentences.l:
but her breast panting,
and her wild heart swells with frenzy;
sentences.i: but her breast heaves, and her wild heart swells with frenzy;
sentences.n: 'Sed' sets up the contrast; 'pectus anhelum' is 'a panting breast', with 'est' omitted. 'Rabie' is an ablative of cause, 'with frenzy', and 'fera corda' is a plural for one heart, 'wild heart'. 'Tument' is 'swell'.

sentences.t:
maiorque videri,
nec mortale sonans, adflata est numine quando
iam propiore dei.
sentences.l:
and greater to look at, nor sounding anything mortal,
since she has been breathed on by the divine power
of the god now nearer.
sentences.i: She seems taller, her voice no longer a mortal voice, since the power of the god, now closer, has breathed on her.
sentences.n: 'Maior videri' is 'greater to be seen', an infinitive of respect (a Greek construction), 'in appearance'. 'Nec mortale sonans' is 'not sounding anything mortal', with 'mortale' a neuter accusative used as an adverb. 'Adflata est numine' is 'has been breathed on by the divine power'; 'quando' is causal, 'since'. 'Propiore' is an ablative comparative, 'nearer', agreeing with 'numine'; 'iam' is 'now'.

sentences.t:
“Cessas in vota precesque,
“Tros ait Aenea?
sentences.l:
“Do you hesitate over vows and prayers,
Trojan,” she says, “Aeneas?
sentences.i: “Do you hang back from vows and prayers, Trojan Aeneas?” she says.
sentences.n: The print has '“Cessas in vota precesque, / “Tros ait Aenea?', an opening mark before 'Tros', a misprint for 'Cessas in vota precesque, Tros” ait “Aenea?': the closing mark belongs after 'Tros' and a fresh opening mark before 'Aenea', since 'Tros… Aenea' is one vocative with 'ait' dropped into it. t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l breaks the speech after 'Trojan' as the Latin does, and i, for the sake of English, closes it after 'Aeneas?' and opens it again at 31. 'Cessas' is 'you linger', 'you hang back', and 'in vota precesque' is 'when it comes to vows and prayers'. 'Tros… Aenea' is a vocative, 'Trojan Aeneas'; 'Aenea' is the Greek vocative.

sentences.t: Cessas?
sentences.l: Do you hesitate?
sentences.i: “Do you hang back?
sentences.n: The repeated 'cessas?' is a sharp second question, 'do you linger?'. The speech is still open here and runs to the end of 53.

sentences.t:
Neque enim ante dehiscent
attonitae magna ora domus.
sentences.l:
For not before will the great mouths
of the thunderstruck house gape.”
sentences.i: For the great mouths of the house, struck dumb with awe, will not gape open until you do.”
sentences.n: The print has 'domus. ”Et', the closing mark of the Sibyl's speech set after a space and joined to the next word, a misprint for 'domus.” Et'; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source (the mark stands at the head of the next unit); l and i close the speech after 'domus.'. 'Neque enim' is 'for… not', 'ante' an adverb, 'before that'. 'Dehiscent' is a future, 'will gape open'. 'Attonitae… domus' is 'of the thunderstruck house', 'attonitae' a perfect participle passive agreeing with 'domus' (genitive); 'magna ora' are 'the great mouths', the hundred doors.

sentences.t:
”Et talia fata
conticuit.
sentences.l:
And having spoken such things
she fell silent.
sentences.i: With those words she fell silent.
sentences.n: The mark ” before 'Et' is the misprinted closing mark of her speech (see the note on the previous unit). 'Fata' here is the perfect participle of 'for', 'having spoken' (nominative feminine, agreeing with the Sibyl), not 'fata', 'the fates', the noun of 45. 'Conticuit' is 'fell silent', a perfect.

sentences.t:
Gelidus Teucris per dura cucurrit
ossa tremor, funditque preces rex pectore ab imo:
sentences.l:
An icy shudder ran through the hard bones
of the Teucrians, and the king pours out prayers from the bottom of his breast:
sentences.i: A chill shudder ran through the Trojans' hard bones, and the king pours out his prayers from the depth of his heart:
sentences.n: 'Gelidus… tremor' is 'an icy tremor'; 'Teucris' is a dative of reference, 'for the Teucrians', and 'per dura… ossa' is 'through the hard bones', with the verb set between adjective and noun. 'Cucurrit' is the perfect of 'curro'. 'Rex' is Aeneas. 'Pectore ab imo' is 'from the lowest breast', 'from the bottom of his heart'. The colon leads to his prayer, which runs to 76.

sentences.t:
“Phoebe, graves Troiae semper miserate labores,
Dardana qui Paridis direxti tela manusque
corpus in Aeacidae,
sentences.l:
“Phoebus, who always pitied the heavy labours of Troy,
who directed the Dardan missiles and the hand of Paris
at the body of the Aeacid,
sentences.i: “Phoebus, who have always felt for the heavy sufferings of Troy, who guided the Trojan arrows and the hand of Paris against the body of Aeacus's grandson,
sentences.n: A new paragraph; the opening mark begins Aeneas's prayer. 'Miserate' is a vocative of the perfect participle of the deponent 'miseror', 'you who have pitied', used as an adjective with 'semper'. 'Graves… labores' is 'the heavy labours' (the Latin Library prints 'gravis', the same case). 'Direxti' is the syncopated 'direxisti' (the Latin Library prints 'derexti'). 'Dardana… tela' is 'Dardan weapons', Trojan arrows, and 'manusque' is 'and the hand'; the plural 'manus' is used for one hand. 'Aeacidae' is the genitive of the patronymic 'Aeacides', 'of the descendant of Aeacus', Achilles (Aeacus was his grandfather); Apollo guided Paris's arrow to Achilles's heel. The sentence goes on.

sentences.t:
magnas obeuntia terras
tot maria intravi duce te, penitusque repostas
Massylum gentes praetentaque Syrtibus arva,
sentences.l:
circling great lands,
so many seas I entered, you as my guide, and far withdrawn
the Massylian peoples, and the fields stretched before the Syrtes,
sentences.i: I have entered so many seas that wash great lands, with you to guide me, and the far-withdrawn peoples of the Massylians, and the fields that lie in front of the Syrtes,
sentences.n: 'Obeuntia' is a present participle, neuter plural, agreeing with 'maria', 'going round', 'skirting' great lands. 'Intravi' is a perfect, 'I have entered', and 'duce te' is an ablative absolute, 'you as guide'. 'Repostas' is the syncopated 'repositas', 'laid away', agreeing with 'gentes' (Latin Library 'gentis', the same case); 'penitus' means 'deep within'. 'Massylum' is an old genitive plural in '-um' (you'll see this constantly); the Massylians are a people of North Africa. 'Praetenta' is a perfect participle passive of 'praetendo', 'stretched in front of', with 'Syrtibus' as a dative; the Syrtes are the shoals and quicksands off the African coast.

sentences.t: iam tandem Italiae fugientis prendimus oras;
sentences.l: now at last we take hold of the shores of fleeing Italy;
sentences.i: now at last we lay hold of the shores of Italy that kept slipping away;
sentences.n: 'Prendimus' is the shortened form of 'prehendimus', 'we grasp'. 'Italiae fugientis' is 'of fleeing Italy', Italy that always seemed to recede.

sentences.t: hac Troiana tenus fuerit Fortuna secuta.
sentences.l: thus far let Trojan Fortune have followed.
sentences.i: May the ill fortune of Troy have followed us only to this point.
sentences.n: 'Hac… tenus' is 'thus far', 'tenus' placed after its word. 'Fuerit… secuta' is a perfect subjunctive of the deponent 'sequor', a wish or an order, 'let her have followed': 'Fortuna' is personified and 'Troiana' marks it as the fortune that attached to Troy. The wish is that her pursuit end here.

sentences.t:
Vos quoque Pergameae iam fas est parcere genti,
dique deaeque omnes quibus obstitit Ilium et ingens
gloria Dardaniae.
sentences.l:
You also, it is now right to spare the Pergamean race,
gods and goddesses all, to whom Ilium and the great
glory of Dardania stood in the way.
sentences.i: You also, all gods and goddesses in whose way Ilium and the great glory of Dardania stood, it is now right that you spare the Trojan nation.
sentences.n: 'Vos quoque' means the gods in general, now added to Phoebus ('you also'). 'Fas est' is 'it is right (by divine law)', followed by 'parcere' with the dative 'genti', 'to spare'. 'Pergameae' is 'of Pergamum', Troy's citadel. 'Dique deaeque' is 'and gods and goddesses', 'dique' being 'diique', the nominative plural of 'deus' with '-que'. 'Quibus obstitit' is 'to whom (Ilium and the great glory) was an obstacle', with the singular verb for two subjects and the dative 'quibus'; 'Dardaniae' is genitive, 'of Dardania', a name of Troy.

sentences.t:
Tuque, O sanctissima vates,
praescia venturi, da, non indebita posco
regna meis fatis, Latio considere Teucros
errantisque deos agitataque numina Troiae.
sentences.l:
And you, O most holy seer,
foreknowing what is to come, grant (I ask no kingdoms not owed
to my fates) that the Teucrians settle in Latium,
and the wandering gods and harried divinities of Troy.
sentences.i: And you, most holy prophetess, who see ahead, grant (I claim no realm that is not owed to my destiny) that the Trojans settle in Latium, with their wandering gods and the storm-driven powers of Troy.
sentences.n: 'Tuque, O sanctissima vates' is a vocative; 'praescia venturi' is 'foreknowing what is to come', 'venturi' a genitive neuter of the future participle. 'Da… considere Teucros' is 'grant that the Teucrians settle', an accusative and infinitive after 'da'. 'Non indebita posco regna meis fatis' is a parenthesis, 'I ask no kingdoms not owed to my fates': 'non indebita' is a litotes, a negative that means 'owed', and 'meis fatis' is a dative. 'Latio' is 'in Latium'. 'Errantisque deos' is 'wandering gods' ('errantis' is the accusative plural in '-is'); 'agitataque numina Troiae' are 'the harried divinities of Troy', the Trojan household gods carried from the ruins.

sentences.t:
Tum Phoebo et Triviae solido de marmore templum
instituam, festosque dies de nomine Phoebi.
sentences.l:
Then to Phoebus and Trivia of solid marble a temple
I will establish, and festal days from the name of Phoebus.
sentences.i: Then I will found for Phoebus and Trivia a temple of solid marble, and festival days called by the name of Phoebus.
sentences.n: 'Instituam' is a future, 'I will establish', taking both 'templum' and 'dies'. 'Solido de marmore' is 'of solid marble', with the preposition between the words. 'Festos dies de nomine Phoebi' is 'festal days named from Phoebus', a festival which the Romans kept for Apollo.

sentences.t: Te quoque magna manent regnis penetralia nostris:
sentences.l: You also great inner shrines await in my kingdoms:
sentences.i: You too will have great shrines waiting in my realm:
sentences.n: 'Te' is the object of 'manent', 'await'. 'Magna… penetralia' is 'great inner shrines'; 'regnis… nostris' is 'in my realms' (the plural is poetic). The colon leads to the reason.

sentences.t:
hic ego namque tuas sortes arcanaque fata,
dicta meae genti, ponam, lectosque sacrabo,
alma, viros.
sentences.l:
For here I will set your oracles and the secret fates
told to my people, and will consecrate chosen
men, kindly one.
sentences.i: For here I shall lay up your oracles and the hidden destinies that were told to my people, and shall consecrate chosen men, gracious one.
sentences.n: 'Namque' is 'for'. 'Sortes' are 'oracular lots', the oracles. 'Arcanaque fata dicta meae genti' is 'the secret fates spoken to my people', 'dicta' a perfect participle passive. 'Ponam' is a future, 'I will set up', and 'lectos… viros' is 'chosen men' as priests ('sacrabo' is 'I will consecrate'). 'Alma' is a vocative, 'kindly one', set between 'lectos' and 'viros'.

sentences.t:
Foliis tantum ne carmina manda,
ne turbata volent rapidis ludibria ventis;
sentences.l:
Only do not entrust songs to leaves,
lest they fly off disordered, playthings for the swift winds;
sentences.i: Only, do not commit your verses to leaves, lest they fly off scattered, a plaything for the rushing winds;
sentences.n: 'Ne… manda' is a prohibition with 'ne' and the imperative, a poetic form (ordinary prose would use 'noli' or 'ne mandaveris'). 'Foliis tantum' is 'only to leaves': the Sibyl wrote her oracles on leaves, which the wind could scatter. 'Ne… volent' is a negative purpose clause, 'lest they fly'; 'volent' is the present subjunctive of 'volo, -are', 'fly', not the future of 'volo, velle'. 'Turbata' is a perfect participle passive, 'thrown into disorder', and 'ludibria' is a neuter plural, 'playthings', 'sport'.

sentences.t: ipsa canas oro.
sentences.l: you yourself sing, I ask.”
sentences.i: Sing them yourself, I beg.”
sentences.n: The print has 'oro. ”Finem', the closing mark of Aeneas's prayer set after a space and joined to the next word, a misprint for 'oro.” Finem'; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source (the mark stands at the head of the next unit); l and i close the prayer after 'oro.'. 'Ipsa canas oro' is 'I ask that you yourself sing': 'canas' is a present subjunctive after 'oro' with 'ut' left out. 'Ipsa' stresses that she must speak in her own voice.

sentences.t: ”Finem dedit ore loquendi.
sentences.l: An end he gave with his mouth of speaking.
sentences.i: With that he put an end to his speaking.
sentences.n: The mark ” before 'Finem' is the misprinted closing mark of Aeneas's prayer (see the note on the previous unit). 'Finem dedit ore loquendi' is 'put an end of speaking with his mouth', the gerund 'loquendi' a genitive with 'finem'. The subject is Aeneas, held over from the prayer.

sentences.i: But in the cave the monstrous seer, not yet able to bear Phoebus, rages and tries to throw the great god from her breast;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Phoebi nondum patiens' is 'not yet bearing Phoebus', 'patiens' taking a genitive. 'Immanis' is 'huge', 'monstrous', nominative singular feminine. 'Bacchatur' is 'raves as a Bacchante'. 'Vates' is feminine here, the Sibyl. 'Si possit' is a subjunctive after 'si', 'in the hope that she may', an implied purpose, and 'excussisse' is a perfect infinitive, 'to have shaken off'. 'Magnum… deum' frames 'pectore', 'from her breast'.

sentences.t:
tanto magis ille fatigat
os rabidum, fera corda domans, fingitque premendo.
sentences.l:
so much the more he wears out her raving mouth,
taming the wild heart, and shapes her by pressing.
sentences.i: so much the harder does the god wear down her frenzied mouth, mastering her wild heart, and moulds her by pressure.
sentences.n: 'Tanto magis' is 'so much the more', an ablative of degree of difference. 'Ille' is the god. 'Os rabidum' is 'the raving mouth', and 'fera corda domans' is 'taming the wild heart'. 'Fingit… premendo' is 'shapes by pressing', the ablative of the gerund, a picture of the god bridling a wild horse or kneading clay.

sentences.t:
Ostia iamque domus patuere ingentia centum
sponte sua, vatisque ferunt responsa per auras:
sentences.l:
And now the hundred huge mouths of the house have opened
of their own accord, and carry the answers of the seer through the air:
sentences.i: And now the hundred huge doors of the house have flown open by themselves and carry the seer's answers out upon the air:
sentences.n: 'Patuere' is 'patuerunt', 'lay open'. 'Ostia… ingentia centum' is 'a hundred huge doors'; 'sponte sua' is 'of their own accord'. 'Ferunt' is 'carry', with the doors as the subject, 'through the air'; 'vatis… responsa' is 'the seer's answers'. The colon leads to her speech, which runs to 97.

sentences.t: “O tandem magnis pelagi defuncte periclis!
sentences.l: “O you who have at last finished with the great dangers of the sea!
sentences.i: “You who have come at last through the great perils of the sea!
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the opening mark begins the Sibyl's answer. 'Defuncte' is a vocative of the perfect participle of the deponent 'defungor', 'having done with', and takes the ablative 'periclis'. 'Pelagi' is a genitive, 'of the sea'.

sentences.t: Sed terrae graviora manent.
sentences.l: But heavier things remain on land.
sentences.i: But on the land there are still heavier things in store.
sentences.n: 'Graviora' is a neuter plural comparative, 'heavier things', and 'manent' is 'await'. 'Terrae' is either a locative, 'on land', or a genitive, 'of the land'; it is set against 'pelagi' above.

sentences.t:
In regna Lavini
Dardanidae venient;
sentences.l:
Into the kingdoms of Lavinium
the Dardanidae will come;
sentences.i: The sons of Dardanus will come into the realm of Lavinium;
sentences.n: 'Lavini' is the genitive of 'Lavinium', 'of Lavinium'. 'Dardanidae' is 'sons of Dardanus', the Trojans, a nominative plural in the Greek form. 'Venient' is a future.

sentences.t: mitte hanc de pectore curam;
sentences.l: put aside this care from your heart;
sentences.i: put this anxiety out of your heart;
sentences.n: 'Mitte' is an imperative, 'dismiss', 'let go', and 'de pectore' is 'from the heart'. 'Hanc… curam' is 'this care', the worry about reaching Italy.

sentences.t: sed non et venisse volent.
sentences.l: but they will not also wish to have come.
sentences.i: but they will wish they had never come.
sentences.n: 'Sed non et venisse volent' is 'but they will not also wish to have come': 'volent' is the future of 'volo, velle', 'will wish', with the perfect infinitive 'venisse', and 'et' is 'also', 'even', so 'they will not be glad, after coming, to have come'. The sense is 'they will regret it'.

sentences.t:
Bella, horrida bella,
et Thybrim multo spumantem sanguine cerno.
sentences.l:
Wars, horrid wars,
and Thybris foaming with much blood I see.
sentences.i: Wars I see, grim wars, and the Tiber foaming with streams of blood.
sentences.n: 'Bella, horrida bella' is a repetition with an adjective between, 'wars, horrid wars', both the object of 'cerno', 'I see'. 'Thybrim' is an accusative in '-im', and 'multo… sanguine' is an ablative of cause or means, 'with much blood'; 'spumantem' is a present participle, 'foaming'. A seer's vision of the war to come.

sentences.t:
Non Simois tibi, nec Xanthus, nec Dorica castra
defuerint;
sentences.l:
Not a Simois for you, nor a Xanthus, nor Dorian camps
will have been lacking;
sentences.i: You will not lack a Simois, or a Xanthus, or Greek encampments;
sentences.n: 'Non… nec… nec' is 'neither… nor… nor'. 'Defuerint' is a future perfect, 'will have failed', with the dative 'tibi', 'for you'. The Simois and the Xanthus are the rivers of Troy: the sense is that the war on the Italian rivers will repeat the one at Troy, and 'Dorica castra' are 'Dorian', Greek, camps. The Greeks of Troy have their counterparts in the Italian enemies.

sentences.t:
alius Latio iam partus Achilles,
natus et ipse dea;
sentences.l:
another Achilles already born for Latium,
himself too the son of a goddess;
sentences.i: a second Achilles is already born in Latium, he too the child of a goddess;
sentences.n: 'Alius… Achilles' is 'another Achilles', a prediction of Turnus, though he is not named. 'Partus' is a perfect participle passive of 'pario', 'brought forth', and 'Latio' is 'in Latium'. 'Natus et ipse dea' is 'he himself also born of a goddess', 'dea' an ablative of origin: Achilles's mother was Thetis.

sentences.t:
nec Teucris addita Iuno
usquam aberit;
sentences.l:
nor will Juno, set against the Teucrians,
be absent anywhere;
sentences.i: nor will Juno, fastened upon the Trojans, be absent anywhere;
sentences.n: 'Addita' is a perfect participle passive, 'attached', 'added', agreeing with Iuno; 'Teucris' is a dative, 'to the Teucrians'. 'Nec… usquam aberit' is 'nor will she be absent anywhere', 'aberit' a future.

sentences.t:
cum tu supplex in rebus egenis
quas gentes Italum aut quas non oraveris urbes!
sentences.l:
when you, a suppliant in need,
what peoples of the Italians, or what cities will you not have begged!
sentences.i: And you, a suppliant in your need: what peoples of Italy, what cities, will you not have begged for help!
sentences.n: 'Cum' is 'when', 'in rebus egenis' is 'in needy circumstances', and 'supplex' is a predicative adjective, 'as a suppliant'. 'Quas gentes Italum aut quas non oraveris urbes!' is an exclamatory question, 'what peoples of the Italians, or what cities will you not have begged!', 'oraveris' being a future perfect (a perfect subjunctive is also possible). 'Italum' is an old genitive plural in '-um' (you'll see this constantly).

sentences.t:
Causa mali tanti coniunx iterum hospita Teucris
externique iterum thalami.
sentences.l:
The cause of so great an evil a wife again a guest to the Teucrians,
and again a foreign marriage.
sentences.i: The cause of so great a woe is a foreign bride once more, a stranger among the Trojans, and once more a marriage with an outsider.
sentences.n: 'Causa mali tanti' is 'the cause of so great an evil', with 'est' omitted. 'Coniunx… hospita' is 'a wife… foreign': 'hospita' is a feminine adjective, 'of a stranger', 'foreign', and 'Teucris' is a dative of reference, 'for the Teucrians'; the 'coniunx' is the bride to come. 'Externi… thalami' is nominative plural, 'and a foreign marriage', the second thing named as the cause with 'coniunx', and 'iterum' ('again') is said twice, a comparison with Helen and the war of Troy. The coming bride is Lavinia, though she is not named. Line 94, 'externique iterum thalami', is a half-line: Virgil left it unfinished, and Greenough prints it short.

sentences.t:
Tu ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito,
qua tua te Fortuna sinet.
sentences.l:
You, do not yield to evils, but go against them more boldly,
where your Fortune will allow you.
sentences.i: Do not give way before your misfortunes, but go to meet them with a bolder heart, by whatever road your fortune lets you.
sentences.n: 'Ne cede' is a prohibition with 'ne' and the imperative, as at 74. 'Malis' is a dative with 'cede', 'to evils'. 'Contra… audentior ito' is 'go against them more boldly', with 'ito' a future imperative of 'eo' and 'audentior' a comparative nominative, 'more daring'. 'Qua… sinet' is 'where she will allow', 'sinet' a future of 'sino', and 'Fortuna' is personified.

sentences.t:
Via prima salutis,
quod minime reris, Graia pandetur ab urbe.”
sentences.l:
The first way of safety, what you least expect,
will be opened from a Greek city.”
sentences.i: Your first road to safety, though you could never guess it, will lie open from a city of the Greeks.”
sentences.n: 'Via prima salutis' is 'the first road of safety'. 'Quod minime reris' is 'which you least think', with 'quod' referring to the whole thought and 'reris' the second singular of the deponent 'reor'. 'Graia… ab urbe' is 'from a Greek city', with the preposition set between adjective and noun, an unnamed city (it will prove to be Evander's Pallanteum). 'Pandetur' is a future passive, 'will be opened'. The closing mark ends the Sibyl's speech.
